I am excited to explore space technology, data science and applying AI to solve real-world problems.

For this NASA Space Apps Challenge, I'm excited to collaborate with everyone, exchange ideas, and build something innovative together. Looking forward to working with you all!.
summary:
We built Selene to help users answer two connected questions: where on the Moon could a surface mission operate, and when would conditions be suitable? Users can select a location on an interactive 3D lunar atlas, choose a date range, and examine sunlight, darkness, Earth visibility, estimated surface temperature and terrain information. Selene can also search for operating windows that match mission requirements.

For example, a team exploring Connecting Ridge near the lunar south pole can identify periods when Earth is visible, estimate how long equipment may depend on batteries, and compare possible mission dates. The platform also provides site comparisons, engineering calculators and downloadable results.

Selene is designed for students, educators and early mission-concept teams. It clearly presents its data sources, assumptions, model limitations and missing information, helping users understand not only the result, but also how it was produced.
details:
A lunar landing site is only useful if it can support the mission during the planned stay. A ridge may receive sunlight for much of the year, yet a particular visit could still include a long period of darkness or limited visibility of Earth. We built Selene so users can evaluate a location, a date range, and a set of mission requirements together.

Users begin by selecting a named site on a 3D Moon or entering lunar coordinates. The forecast shows how sunlight, Earth visibility, and estimated surface temperature change over the selected period. A team can compare Connecting Ridge with another south-polar site over the same dates, then use the science-window and mission-operations tools to find candidate periods that meet its requirements. Solar-power and battery calculators connect those results to a practical question: how much energy storage might the equipment need during the longest dark interval?

We built the interface with React, TypeScript, and Three.js, and the scientific backend with Python and FastAPI. The Agent Swarm feature organizes planning into stages, from choosing a site to considering surface operations. A Groq-backed chatbot helps users navigate the tools and express planning questions in everyday language. The backend performs the numerical calculations, and users can export results for comparison or further analysis.

Selene makes the assumptions behind a candidate window visible. The hosted version uses built-in approximations where full scientific datasets are unavailable. Earth visibility indicates whether Earth is above the modeled horizon; an actual radio link also depends on the communications equipment. Likewise, the forecast samples conditions at intervals, so brief interruptions can fall between samples. By showing these limits alongside the results, Selene gives students and early mission teams a way to explain why they chose a site, what their choice depends on, and what they would investigate next.
